cards.title: Build Audience Before Pitching Big-Box Retail
cards.summary: Retail buyers back brands with proven, large-scale customer recognition, so grow a digital audience first and use sell-through as your proof.
cards.use_when: Deciding when to pitch a national retailer (Target, Kohl's, etc.) or evaluating whether you have enough demand signal to pursue wholesale.

cards.title: Localize Creative and Site for International Rollout
cards.summary: International expansion failed when turned on without localization; fix it by translating the site and re-shooting proven creative with local talent in native languages.
cards.use_when: Planning or fixing international expansion — deciding which markets to enter and what to localize before launch.

cards.title: Slow Down on Customer-Facing Rollouts
cards.summary: The source's 'fail fast' ethos worked internally but should not apply to customer-facing launches like international, where go-slow testing is warranted.
cards.use_when: Deciding rollout pace for a customer-facing change — new market, new website experience, new storefront channel.

cards.title: Hire a Scaling CFO Early for Forecasting and Profitability Discipline
cards.summary: A CFO who can grow with the company, build rolling forecasts and models, and enforce profitability avoids the over-spend, burn-and-raise trap.
cards.use_when: Deciding when to bring on senior finance leadership and how to govern spend, forecasting, and fundraising.

cards.title: Prevent Over-Buying Inventory Against Unrealistic Revenue Forecasts
cards.summary: The source's darkest days came from ordering inventory against revenue assumptions that didn't materialize, leaving them unable to pay vendors on time.
cards.use_when: Setting inventory buy quantities and negotiating payment terms with suppliers or manufacturers.

cards.title: Validate New Products With Real User Testing Before Launch
cards.summary: True Classic kills products the market rejects — including three failed women's attempts — and scrutinizes every product (wash tests, fit, flow) before shipping.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch a new product category or SKU (women's line, denim, cologne, watches).

cards.title: Target a Price-Margin White Space With a Better-Value Product
cards.summary: True Classic was built on a white space where incumbents overcharged while under-delivering on fit and comfort; the same lens drives new categories.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a new product category or repositioning an existing one by analyzing competitor pricing versus delivered quality.

cards.title: Expand Into Adjacent Categories by Building a Better Product
cards.summary: The founder cites Ridge (wallet → luggage) to argue that a strong product beats category-demo objections; True Classic applies this to denim, cologne, watches, backpacks.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to extend a store into an adjacent category outside your core product or demographic.

cards.title: Tier Your Product Line to Move Customers Up-Market
cards.summary: Launch an elevated version of a core product at a higher price point to serve an 'occasion' use case (going-out shirt) instead of undercutting your base item.
cards.use_when: Planning product line architecture and pricing tiers around a best-selling core SKU.

cards.title: Use AI Personalized Video in Post-Purchase and Welcome Flows
cards.summary: The source describes AI tools that inject the customer's name into founder-recorded video to make welcome/post-purchase emails feel personal at scale.
cards.use_when: Designing welcome and post-purchase email flows for a store where founder personality or brand trust is a differentiator.

cards.title: Prioritize Curiosity and Creativity Over Pure Data Focus
cards.summary: The founder argues curiosity and creative problem-solving outproduce narrow data-driven intelligence, because smart operators can get trapped in the obvious answer.
cards.use_when: Building a team or making strategic decisions where data points to one answer but the market may reward a non-obvious move.

cards.title: Choose Tools That Simplify Operations, Not Just Add Features
cards.summary: The founder prioritizes Shopify for simplicity and describes a core stack (analytics, post-purchase surveys, email/retention) for running a DTC apparel brand.
cards.use_when: Evaluating or selecting storefront, analytics, and retention tooling for a scaling DTC brand.

cards.title: Diversify Acquisition Across Channels With a Facebook Core
cards.summary: The source runs Facebook as the core acquisition channel while spreading spend across additional channels, using post-purchase surveys and analytics to understand true sources.
cards.use_when: Allocating paid acquisition budget across channels for a DTC brand.

cards.title: Test New Sales Channels Before Scaling
cards.summary: The source treats any new channel (retail, Amazon, wholesale) as a toe-dip test: measure results, then ramp only if it works.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether and how fast to add a new sales channel (marketplace, wholesale, physical retail).

cards.title: Build an in-house creator scouting team instead of hiring an agency
cards.summary: Staff a 15–25 person in-house team of scouts who resemble your customer avatar to source and manage TikTok/Instagram influencers directly, as Bloom does with 85% of spend on creators.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to run influencer/creator acquisition through an agency, a freelancer, or an internal team for your store's top-of-funnel content.

cards.title: Use VPNs to break regional algorithm bubbles when sourcing creators
cards.summary: Bloom's scouts use VPNs to shift their own feed geography, surfacing localized creators such as a mom in Kansas or a policewoman in North Carolina who would never appear in a coastal-city feed.
cards.use_when: Your influencer sourcing pipeline keeps returning the same handful of urban creators and you need genuinely diverse, regionally distributed voices for acquisition content.

cards.title: Price flat creator fees by reverse-engineering a target CPM
cards.summary: Instead of paying per post arbitrarily, set creator flat fees from a target CPM derived from your paid-social benchmark — Bloom halves Meta's CPM (e.g. $20 Meta → $10 creator target) and claims sub-$2 CPM outcomes on some deals.
cards.use_when: You are negotiating or budgeting creator/influencer flat fees and need a defensible per-video price rather than gut feel.

cards.title: Discount creator payouts for off-target audience demographics
cards.summary: Bloom adjusts flat fees down when a creator's audience skews away from the target customer — e.g. cutting pay 25% if 25% of the audience is male when the target is female.
cards.use_when: You are setting or renegotiating creator rates and need to price in audience-quality mismatch rather than only reach.

cards.title: Run influencer marketing with no affiliate links or coupon codes
cards.summary: Bloom deliberately avoids attribution links and codes and optimises for pure top-of-funnel awareness, relying on an omni-channel halo rather than last-click tracking.
cards.use_when: You are designing the measurement approach for a creator programme and deciding whether to impose trackable links or codes on creators.

cards.title: Give creators total creative control and avoid a 'lame' brief
cards.summary: Bloom attributes performance to minimal briefs — creators are the experts in their own communities, so the brand supplies product and guardrails rather than scripts.
cards.use_when: You are writing creator briefs for a paid or organic acquisition campaign and deciding how prescriptive to be.

cards.title: Expand TAM by moving from a niche product into saturated, no-education categories
cards.summary: Bloom started with niche products (booty bands, female pre-workout for lifting/anxiety) then stepped up to greens, protein and energy drinks — deliberately choosing saturated categories to avoid spending money on consumer education.
cards.use_when: You are planning the next product line or category expansion for your store and deciding whether to pioneer a new category or enter an existing one.

cards.title: Read community feedback from in-person crowds, not online loud minorities
cards.summary: Bloom sources product and flavor feedback from physical crowd interactions to avoid over-indexing on the vocal keyboard minority that skews online sentiment.
cards.use_when: You are deciding what flavours, variants or product changes to launch next and want a more representative signal than comment sections or reviews.

cards.title: Use 'validity marketing' language such as 'restock' to signal demand
cards.summary: Bloom reports that 'restock' is the most powerful word in its marketing — signalling proven demand and scarcity rather than making a fresh claim — and uses this to attract retail buyers and investors.
cards.use_when: You are writing PDP copy, launch emails or social announcements and want to leverage evidence of real demand instead of discount-led messaging.

cards.title: Host large free in-person events to generate years of digital content
cards.summary: Bloom stages expensive live events (such as taking over a diner in Austin and giving away free meals all weekend) primarily to capture digital B-roll and content that can be reused for years.
cards.use_when: You are planning brand activations or content production and considering whether an in-person event earns its cost through reusable assets.

cards.title: Enter strategic distribution partnerships to solve supply chain without selling the company
cards.summary: Bloom partnered with Nutrabolt (C4) and Dr Pepper for its beverage launch to gain supply chain, logistics and distribution capability while reportedly maintaining 70% ownership and tripling enterprise value.
cards.use_when: You are launching a heavy or complex product (e.g. beverages) and need distribution, logistics or manufacturing partners but want to keep control of your store and brand.

cards.title: Prove retail concept with one chain, then scale doors and protect POs with inventory
cards.summary: Bloom focused on Target to prove the concept, then expanded to roughly 50,000 doors, and deliberately overproduces inventory so it never misses a purchase order from a major retailer.
cards.use_when: You are planning offline retail distribution for your store and need to decide which chain to prove first and how much stock to hold.

cards.title: Humanise relationships with retail buyers to win shelf space
cards.summary: Bloom's retail success came partly from building a relationship with the specific buyer at the retailer rather than anonymous account management.
cards.use_when: You are preparing a buyer pitch or managing an existing retail account and want to strengthen the human relationship that determines shelf space.

cards.title: Apply the '1+1=3' framework when evaluating partnership deals
cards.summary: Bloom evaluates strategic partnerships on whether the combination produces capability neither party could efficiently build alone — as C4/Dr Pepper solved distribution for the beverage launch.
cards.use_when: You are assessing a distribution, manufacturing or retail partnership and want a framework for whether it is genuinely additive.

cards.title: Use TikTok Shop success as a digital-to-retail halo signal
cards.summary: Bloom tracks TikTok Shop sales as a demand engine whose success coincides with lifts on Amazon, Target and Walmart, without using affiliate links to model the effect.
cards.use_when: You are deciding how much to invest in TikTok Shop versus other channels and want to account for its knock-on effect on retail and marketplace sales.

cards.title: Ask candidates which three brands they love and why in hiring
cards.summary: Bloom uses a simple interview question — name three brands you love and why — to assess taste, consumer instinct and brand literacy for ecommerce marketing roles.
cards.use_when: You are hiring for marketing, brand, creative or merchandising roles in your store and want a signal of consumer taste beyond a CV.

cards.title: Build founder personal brand to control deal flow and luck
cards.summary: Greg built a personal brand deliberately to generate inbound opportunities, relationships and high-level connections rather than relying on outbound.
cards.use_when: You want to attract retail buyers, investors, partners or senior hires to your ecommerce brand through the founder's visibility.

cards.title: Use creator content as a paid-social creative pool instead of agency-produced assets
cards.summary: Bloom's high creator volume across TikTok and Instagram (reportedly 15 billion+ views) supplies a pool of native creative that can be used and re-used for paid social.
cards.use_when: You are planning paid-social creative supply and deciding whether to commission creator content or build assets internally/with an agency.

cards.title: Step up TAM ceilings deliberately from niche subsets to mass market
cards.summary: Bloom's sequence — booty bands and female pre-workout for lifting/anxiety, then greens, then protein, then energy drinks — shows a deliberate ladder from niche audiences to mass-market categories.
cards.use_when: You are planning a multi-year product roadmap for your store and want to raise the addressable market ceiling with each launch.

cards.title: Build an In-House Influencer Scouting Team with Diverse Algorithms
cards.summary: Use a team of junior scouts on VPN-diversified social feeds to find creators matching your actual national customer, not just your HQ's local bubble.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing an influencer/affiliate creator-sourcing engine for an ecommerce brand, especially if sourcing feels repetitive or slanted to one region or demographic.

cards.title: Price Influencer Deals Off Your Own Meta CPM, Halved
cards.summary: Reverse-engineer flat influencer payouts from your known Meta CPM, then cut it in half as the initial target so paid creator views beat your paid-ad efficiency.
cards.use_when: Negotiating flat-rate creator deals or setting a target blended CPM for an influencer/affiliate program on an ecommerce brand.

cards.title: Give Creators Product and Creative Control, Not Scripts
cards.summary: Ship free product with minimal brief and let creators explain and use it their own way, because heavy scripts kill the organic reach you are paying for.
cards.use_when: Writing creator briefs and packaging product for an influencer seeding program, or diagnosing why creator content is underperforming.

cards.title: Choose Creator Follower Bands and Platform Mix
cards.summary: Select creator sizes and platforms by budget and goal — the source favors a diverse portfolio and prioritizes a 5k–50k follower band on a limited budget.
cards.use_when: Allocating influencer budget across creator sizes and platforms for an ecommerce brand, or starting a program with limited spend.

cards.title: Segment TikTok Content from TikTok Shop Affiliate
cards.summary: Treat TikTok organic creator content and TikTok Shop affiliate as two distinct programs to master, because affiliate is incremental and community-monetizing rather than a replacement.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch or expand a TikTok Shop affiliate program alongside an existing creator/content program for an ecommerce brand.

cards.title: Accept Correlational Attribution for Top-of-Funnel Creator Spend
cards.summary: If most marketing spend sits at top of funnel for an omni-channel brand, use correlational signals (like Amazon search lift) rather than demanding clean last-click attribution.
cards.use_when: Setting measurement expectations for a large influencer program, especially on an omni-channel brand selling through Amazon, retail doors and DTC at once.

cards.title: Open, Large, Free Events Engineered for Content
cards.summary: Run fewer, bigger, public free events that generate reusable digital content and consumer feedback, rather than many small VIP-only gatherings.
cards.use_when: Planning brand events or activations for an ecommerce brand, and deciding event format, frequency and guest list.

cards.title: Use Live Sampling to Choose Product Flavors and Validate Launches
cards.summary: Sample unreleased products to real customers at events and read the reactions, because small in-person samples beat the loud minority of commenters and syndicated data.
cards.use_when: Deciding on new flavors, SKUs or product launches, especially when feedback comes mainly from comments, surveys or purchased syndicated data.

cards.title: Turn Your Team into a Product Incubation Lab
cards.summary: Hire people who are your target customer and watch what they actually consume and bring into the office as an ongoing product-idea pipeline.
cards.use_when: Sourcing new product or flavor ideas for an ecommerce brand without expensive consumer research.

cards.title: Use 'Restock' Language as a Validity Signal
cards.summary: Restock announcements, bestseller rankings and retailer proof convert skeptics because they borrow proof from repetition and scale that a new brand does not yet have.
cards.use_when: Writing email/SMS drop copy, PDP proof elements or social posts for a product that sold out and restocked, or when trying to build trust as a newer ecommerce brand.

cards.title: Roll Event Revenue Back into Inventory, Not Lifestyle
cards.summary: When a big sales day hits, reinvest the cash into more product rather than personal or discretionary spend, because growth brands are cash-hungry.
cards.use_when: After a spike day, restock, launch or viral moment — deciding how to allocate a large cash inflow in an ecommerce inventory business.

cards.title: Build in Public and Post Verifiable Validation Statements
cards.summary: Share the founder's real, quantified business progress publicly — rankings, retailer wins, restocks — to earn trust, recruit talent and attract retail and investor attention.
cards.use_when: Planning founder-led content, LinkedIn/X/Instagram presence or PR-style announcements to build trust and inbound opportunities for an ecommerce brand.

cards.title: Launch into Saturated Categories to Avoid Paying for Education
cards.summary: Enter categories where demand is already taught and containers are standardized, then win on product, brand and flavor rather than on explaining what the product is.
cards.use_when: Choosing the next product category or launch format for an ecommerce brand, especially when deciding whether to enter a crowded space.

cards.title: Step Up TAM in Sequenced Product Launches
cards.summary: Grow by deliberately moving from niche products with low ceilings to progressively larger categories, using community requests and founder pain points as the guide.
cards.use_when: Deciding the next product line or category expansion for an ecommerce brand with an established customer base.

cards.title: Retain Older Customers for Ritual and Subscription Products
cards.summary: If you sell a daily ritual or subscription product, target buyers with established routines, because younger customers historically retain and subscribe less.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing retention or subscription churn, or choosing the age/psychographic profile to target in acquisition for a supplement, consumable or subscription ecommerce brand.

cards.title: Run a Diverse Portfolio and Let Customers Migrate Within It
cards.summary: Expect individual products to decay while the brand grows, and design the portfolio so customers move to newer products rather than leaving.
cards.use_when: Reviewing product-line performance and deciding whether to sunset, reprioritize or continue supporting declining catalog items in an ecommerce brand.

cards.title: Hire Age and Background Diversity in Marketing Teams
cards.summary: Mix junior scouting with more experienced operational roles, and watch for generational blind spots in what the team considers good creative.
cards.use_when: Structuring an ecommerce marketing, creator or content team, or diagnosing why creative or sourcing skews too young or too local.

cards.title: Scale Creator Programs from Proven Product-Led Virality
cards.summary: Only build a large creator program when the product already drives repeat use and organic content; then treat outreach as the thing to scale.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest heavily in an influencer program, or diagnosing why creator content is not converting into repeat purchase for an ecommerce brand.

cards.title: Choose a Saturated Category, Then Find the White Space Inside It
cards.summary: Bloom's product-selection rule: enter categories that already exist on Amazon and retail shelves, then differentiate on distribution, price, palatability or audience rather than inventing a category.
cards.use_when: Deciding which new product to launch or which category to add to your store's catalog.

cards.title: Raise Your Barrier to Entry With Distribution, Not Just Product
cards.summary: Bloom moved from easy-to-copy supplements to capital- and relationship-intensive channels (retail doors, strategic partners) specifically to make imitation hard.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to invest next — product line, channel or partnership — to protect your store from copycat sellers.

cards.title: Build Demand Before You Ask a Retailer for Shelf Space
cards.summary: Bloom got buyers to call them by manufacturing visible demand (influencers the specific buyer followed, local billboards) so the retailer felt they'd discovered the brand.
cards.use_when: Pitching a retail buyer, marketplace category manager, or wholesale account and needing leverage before the first conversation.

cards.title: Make Partnerships Increase Enterprise Value or Don't Sign
cards.summary: Bloom's test for any strategic partnership: if it doesn't raise the value of your business, sell the whole thing instead.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a distribution deal, joint venture, licensing agreement, or equity investment that touches your store.

cards.title: Handle Retail Exclusivity Carefully: Mostly Shoot Wide
cards.summary: Bloom mostly avoids retailer-exclusive products, using FOMO and brief drama as occasional leverage but keeping the same product available everywhere because digital marketing shows it to everyone.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to create a channel-exclusive SKU, bundle, or variant for a marketplace, retailer, or wholesale partner.

cards.title: Send External Traffic to Amazon to Play Its Algorithm
cards.summary: Bloom deliberately redirected its email, SMS and Instagram audience to Amazon, sacrificing DTC to win on a platform it treats as social media with an algorithm.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to allocate audience and ad spend between your own site and a marketplace.

cards.title: Sell to the Household's Decision-Maker, Not the End User
cards.summary: Bloom targets women as buyers because the mother of the household typically shops and then influences the whole family's consumption.
cards.use_when: Choosing your store's target customer, positioning, and creative for a product the whole household or a partner might use.

cards.title: Win Sell-Through by Showing Up In Person to Buyers
cards.summary: Bloom treats in-person, first-name relationships with retail decision-makers as a consistent variable of success, and reputation for fill rates as the thing that gets you the next door.
cards.use_when: Managing an ongoing wholesale/retail relationship or pitching to add a product to a retailer's assortment.

cards.title: You're Only as Good as the Last Three Months
cards.summary: Retail relationships run on 'what have you done for me lately' — past wins don't earn current favor.
cards.use_when: Planning quarterly merchandising, promotions, and account management for marketplaces or wholesale partners.

cards.title: Bootstrap Deliberately: Fund Growth From Profit and Control the Outcome
cards.summary: Bloom bootstrapped to ~$180M with no outside capital, prioritizing control and optionality over the speed external money can buy.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to raise outside capital, take investment, or fund your store's growth from cash flow.

cards.title: Build a Hire-for-Pain-Points Team So You Keep Doing What You Love
cards.summary: Bloom's talent rule: hire one person per pain point — including work you simply don't enjoy — so you can focus on what you're a 10/10 at.
cards.use_when: Deciding your next key hire and how to structure your own time running the store.

cards.title: Don't Network Early — Become Worth Networking With
cards.summary: The source argues networking is overrated before you've built something (roughly $3–5M in revenue) and that once you do, the network comes to you.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to spend your limited time as an early-stage store owner — events and introductions vs. building and shipping.

cards.title: Relocate Deliberately to Control Your Luck
cards.summary: The source treats geographic location as a lever for entrepreneurship luck, moving repeatedly to where his category's ecosystem lived.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to base your store or team, or where to invest in a physical/hub presence.

cards.title: Use Instant Downloads and Free Community to Validate Before Physical Products
cards.summary: Before Bloom, the founders built a multi-million-dollar PDF-guide business with no COGS by selling instant downloads and training buyers personally to prove demand and build community.
cards.use_when: Validating a new product idea or launching a low-cost digital offer before investing in inventory.

cards.title: Use Talent to Control Luck and Reputation, and Always Fill the PO
cards.summary: Bloom's retail advantage is a supply chain and reputation that lets them say yes when a competitor fails, turning reliability into net-new shelf space.
cards.use_when: Building fulfillment/replenishment reliability and deciding whether to accept a rush or gap order.

cards.title: Stay Cognitively Active by Learning From the Current Playbook
cards.summary: The source's growth habit: study people who executed the exact playbook you want, and surround yourself with young people who use today's tactics.
cards.use_when: Choosing mentors, courses, or advisors when planning a new product launch or channel expansion.

cards.title: Build a Founder Personal Brand as CAC Arbitrage
cards.summary: Founder-led content reaches buyers your product-specific influencers can't, functioning as a cheap acquisition and inbound channel.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to spend founder time on content vs. paid acquisition, or expanding reach into an audience segment your current creator roster doesn't touch.

cards.title: Use Amazon BSR as a Free Demand Barometer
cards.summary: Checking Amazon Best Seller Rank lists daily reveals live US demand shifts across categories.
cards.use_when: Product selection and category research: deciding whether to enter a category, or timing an ad or creator bet against current demand.

cards.title: Use Google Trends to Time Bets and Creator Deals
cards.summary: Google Trends shows live search demand over 24 hours to a decade, letting you check whether a trend or influencer is rising before you spend.
cards.use_when: Acquisition creative and creator/podcast sponsorship decisions, or category selection: validating whether demand is durable before signing a contract.

cards.title: Diversify Sales Channels to Remove Key-Man Risk
cards.summary: After losing its largest retail channel, the source treats over-reliance on any single channel, influencer or name as an existential risk.
cards.use_when: Channel strategy and retention planning: deciding how dependent your store should be on one marketplace, one retailer or one creator.

cards.title: Work in Public to Increase Surface Area for Luck
cards.summary: Posting what you're building creates inbound from people who can change your trajectory — deals, investors and partners you'd never reach cold.
cards.use_when: Acquisition and biz-dev for a store: generating investor, retail, affiliate or partnership inbound without a service-sales motion.

cards.title: Build Proprietary In-House Capability Instead of Renting Agencies
cards.summary: Agencies can be short-term teachers, but the durable play is to learn and then build the function in-house.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to outsource ecommerce marketing, influencer, Amazon or creative functions, or when scaling a lean store team.

cards.title: Hire for Taste: Ask What Brands They Love and Why
cards.summary: The first interview question should test whether the candidate actually understands current digital brand-building.
cards.use_when: Hiring for ecommerce brand, marketing, creative or social roles where taste and cultural fluency drive output.

cards.title: Match Hiring to Stage: Hunger Early, Proven Operators Later
cards.summary: Early on, hire un-brainwashed hungry people; as you scale, bring in people who have seen the operational ceiling.
cards.use_when: Team-building decisions as an ecommerce store grows: whether to hire raw enthusiastic talent or experienced operators.

cards.title: Hire Self-Described Entrepreneurs Who Value Ownership
cards.summary: Define 'entrepreneur' as someone who treats themselves as a company and wants ownership, so they welcome being outgrown.
cards.use_when: Screening for ecommerce team members and leaders, especially when you expect the role to change as the store scales.

cards.title: Move from Doer to Environment-Builder as CEO
cards.summary: As your leadership team outgrows you on every vertical, the CEO's job becomes making talent thrive, not making the calls.
cards.use_when: Leadership and org design for a scaling ecommerce brand: deciding where a founder should and shouldn't intervene.

cards.title: Design a Physical HQ for Creative Output, Not Zoom
cards.summary: Founder-led co-location with an activity-rich space drives creativity that remote calls can't replicate, per the source.
cards.use_when: Workplace and team-location decisions for ecommerce brand, marketing and creative functions; deciding which roles must be in person.

cards.title: Install Positive and Negative Feedback Loops, and Control Emotion
cards.summary: Leaders need both reinforcing and corrective feedback, and should not lead through anger.
cards.use_when: Managing an ecommerce team day-to-day: giving feedback, handling disputes, and modeling tone.

cards.title: Use Talent and Deal Flow as a Luck Multiplier
cards.summary: Visible building compounds into a network of people who can help, which the source treats as a deliberate increase in luck.
cards.use_when: Retention and growth planning: deliberately building networks and visibility to surface partners, hires and opportunities.
